data.title: Upcoming Stock Splits This Week (November 23 to November 27) – Stay Invested
data.description:
Few things on Wall Street can make a stock look cheaper or more expensive overnight without changing its actual value. Stock splits do exactly that, turning one share into several or combining multiple shares into one. The numbers change, but the company's worth doesn't move simply because of the transaction.

For companies whose shares have climbed significantly, a traditional split can offer a practical advantage. By lowering the price of each share while increasing the number outstanding, the company makes its stock more accessible to investors who might hesitate to purchase shares carrying a high price tag.

The reverse approach is often associated with companies facing a much tougher situation. A reverse split raises the individual share price by reducing the number of shares outstanding. While that doesn't improve the company's financial condition, it can help satisfy exchange listing standards and reduce the risk of delisting when shares have traded below required levels.

This makes stock splits something of a window into a company's recent history. A forward split may follow years of gains, while a reverse split can reflect the consequences of a prolonged sell-off. Investors still need to examine the underlying fundamentals to understand what comes next.

So, which companies are about to change the way their shares are counted? Here's a look at the stock splits scheduled for November 23 through November 27, based on TipRanks' Stock Splits Calendar.

Toppoint Holdings (TOPP) – Toppoint Holdings provides trucking and logistics services, specializing in transporting recyclable materials destined for international markets. The company helps move commodities from collection and processing facilities to shipping ports, supporting the recycling export industry. Operations serve customers handling large quantities of reusable materials that require reliable transportation between facilities. On November 13, Toppoint announced a 1-for-5 reverse stock split after NYSE American halted trading in its shares on November 10, citing an abnormally low market price. The move aims to restore an acceptable trading level and support continued exchange listing, with the consolidation targeted for November 23 or shortly thereafter, and split-adjusted trading subject to NYSE American approval.

Algorhythm Holdings (RIME) – Algorhythm Holdings operates through subsidiaries involved in AI, freight transportation, and renewable energy development. Its SemiCab platform uses advanced algorithms to match shipping demand with available trucking capacity, helping transportation operators improve efficiency. Meanwhile, Azure Energy provides advisory services for renewable power projects, expanding the company's reach into energy infrastructure. On November 18, Algorhythm announced a 1-for-10 reverse stock split of its common shares, reducing the outstanding total from about 40.8 million to 4.1 million. The transaction is designed to raise the individual trading price while reducing the share count, with implementation scheduled for November 23.

IM Cannabis (IMCC) – IM Cannabis is a Canada-based medical cannabis company serving patients in Israel through pharmaceutical distribution channels. The company sources and markets regulated cannabis products intended for people receiving physician-supervised treatment. Its commercial activities focus on Israel's established medical marijuana industry, where patients can access prescribed therapies through licensed providers. On November 18, IM Cannabis announced a 1-for-3 reverse stock split of its common shares to help regain compliance with Nasdaq's minimum bid price requirement. The consolidation is scheduled to become effective on November 23, increasing the theoretical price per share while reducing the number of shares outstanding.

Lisata Therapeutics (LSTA) – Lisata Therapeutics is a clinical-stage pharmaceutical company focused on developing experimental medicines for cardioendocrine diseases, while also maintaining an oncology research program. Following its acquisition of Marea Therapeutics, the company's research portfolio includes MAR001, a treatment candidate targeting severe hypertriglyceridemia. Another program, certepetide, aims to improve the delivery of cancer medications into solid tumors. On November 19, Lisata announced a 1-for-15 reverse stock split of its common shares, following investor approval earlier that month. The consolidation comes amid changes to its capital structure associated with the Marea acquisition and related financing, with implementation scheduled for November 23.

Alset (AEI) – Alset is a diversified holding company investing in real estate development, financial services, and technology ventures. Its property activities have included residential communities, while additional investments provide exposure to several other industries. This investment approach allows the group to pursue opportunities beyond traditional property ownership and construction. On November 16, Alset filed an amendment implementing a 1-for-5 reverse stock split of its common shares, combining every five existing shares into one. The transaction will increase the theoretical price per share while reducing the number of shares outstanding, with the adjustment scheduled to take effect on November 23.

Auddia (AUUD) – Auddia develops AI technology designed to change how consumers experience radio, podcasts, and digital audio programming. Its proprietary software recognizes spoken content and enables personalized listening, giving users greater control over their preferred entertainment. The platform also supports audio classification tools that could expand into additional broadcasting applications. On November 19, Auddia announced a 1-for-13.9 reverse stock split of its common shares, following investor authorization in May. The consolidation aims to raise the individual trading price through a reduction in outstanding equity, with adjusted trading scheduled to begin November 23.

Parabolic Technologies (PARA) – Parabolic Technologies, formerly Banzai International, develops AI-powered software that helps companies improve sales productivity, customer engagement, and digital content creation. Its portfolio includes ConnectAndSell, a sales acceleration platform, alongside Demio, OpenReel, and CreateStudio, which support webinars, video production, and marketing activities. These tools serve organizations seeking to automate customer interactions and simplify their commercial operations. On November 19, Parabolic announced a 1-for-100 reverse stock split of its common shares to regain compliance with Nasdaq's minimum bid price requirement. The consolidation is scheduled for November 23, marking the third such transaction in 2026, following a 1-for-20 adjustment in May and another 1-for-10 reduction in October.

Smartkem (SMTK) – Smartkem develops advanced semiconductor materials designed to support the next generation of electronic displays. Its organic transistor technology could enable manufacturers to create flexible, lightweight, and energy-efficient screens for wearable devices and other electronics. The company's proposed merger with Ferrox Critical Minerals could also introduce exposure to titanium and industrial materials. On November 19, Smartkem announced a 1-for-5 reverse stock split of its common shares to support continued Nasdaq listing compliance. The transaction became legally effective on November 20, with adjusted trading scheduled for November 23, following an earlier 1-for-50 consolidation completed in August 2026.

Stratum Holdings (SRTM) – Stratum Holdings is a technology company transitioning from real estate services into AI infrastructure and high-performance computing. Its operations include leasing advanced Nvidia GPUs to organizations requiring computing capacity for AI development and other intensive applications. The company is also pursuing the sale of its legacy real estate operations as it expands its computing infrastructure activities. On November 19, Stratum announced a 1-for-9 reverse stock split of its common shares, reducing the outstanding total from about 5.9 million to 656,000. The adjustment raises the nominal trading price while lowering the equity count, with implementation scheduled for November 23.

iSpecimen (ISPC) – iSpecimen operates an online marketplace connecting medical researchers with healthcare organizations that supply biological samples for scientific studies. Its platform helps laboratories obtain human tissue, blood, and other specimens needed for drug development, diagnostic testing, and disease research. By connecting research institutions with participating providers, the service simplifies the process of sourcing materials for clinical investigations. On November 19, iSpecimen announced a 1-for-6 reverse stock split of its common shares, following investor approval in October and a board decision on November 11. The move comes amid efforts to address Nasdaq listing requirements, reducing outstanding equity from about 5.8 million units to 965,000, with legal implementation scheduled for November 23 and adjusted trading beginning November 24.

Co-Diagnostics (CODX) – Co-Diagnostics develops molecular testing technologies that detect genetic material associated with infectious diseases and other medical conditions. Its proprietary diagnostic platform uses DNA and RNA analysis to detect pathogens, while the Co-Dx PCR system aims to bring laboratory-grade testing closer to patients. These innovations could make diagnostic services more accessible through point-of-care and home testing applications. On November 19, Co-Diagnostics announced a 1-for-25 reverse stock split of its common shares to regain compliance with Nasdaq's $1 minimum bid price requirement while preserving sufficient authorized equity for potential financing. The consolidation is scheduled to take effect on November 24, increasing the individual trading price through a proportional reduction in outstanding units.

Jaguar Health (JAGX) – Jaguar Health develops plant-based prescription medicines targeting gastrointestinal conditions affecting both humans and animals. Its pharmaceutical research focuses on naturally occurring compounds, including treatments for diarrhea associated with chronic illnesses and medical therapies. The company also pursues additional applications for patients experiencing digestive complications during cancer treatment. On November 20, Jaguar announced a 1-for-25 reverse stock split of its common shares to support compliance with Nasdaq's continued listing standards. The consolidation is scheduled for November 24, when adjusted trading will begin following the reduction in outstanding equity.

To find more information about historical and upcoming stock splits, visit the TipRanks Stock Splits Calendar.

data.title: Market Currents: NVISIONING the Bottom?
data.description:
The terrible, horrible, no good, very bad week for stocks: the AI trade loses its Godfather, chips lose their loopholes, and Anthropic's debut loses its pop.

Stocks suffered a brutal selloff, notching one of their worst weeks outside of recessions. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) declined for the fifth straight day on Friday, wrapping up the weekly loss of 8.02%. The S&P 500 (SPX) logged its deepest seven-day slide since February 2020, including the weekly drop of 8.61%. The Nasdaq-100 (NDX) tumbled 10.43% – one of the largest weekly declines in the past 40 years – with much of that loss attributed to Friday's broad selloff in technology stocks. The large-cap tech index is on the verge of a bear market, having lost 19.8% since its October 6 peak. The extent of the selloff has erased nearly all of the year-to-date gains of the DJIA and the S&P 500, while pushing the Nasdaq-100 into the red.

Roughly 40% of the market cap loss in the S&P 500 since its recent high is attributable to NVIDIA (NVDA). The AI chip giant erased $905 billion in market cap over the past week alone, and about $2.8 trillion since October 6. Despite a near-perfect beat-and-raise, the chip leader – reporting for the first time in its 33-year history without Jensen Huang – failed to soothe investor fears regarding both its own future and the broad AI ecosystem. Operationally and financially, NVIDIA's report was more than stellar, with the guidance upgrade reflecting soaring demand alongside improving supply availability.

However, what past results and near-term guidance revealed was already known, and that's part of the problem. The quarter reaffirmed the extraordinary strength of the technological and strategic roadmap built and implemented by Jensen Huang with such brilliance that it now allows the most important tech company in the world not only to chug along, but to accelerate into the next fiscal year. Beyond that horizon, however, no one knows how much of NVIDIA's technological leadership depended on Huang's personal ability to anticipate and shape technological change – or how much of that capability the company retains without him. That's why the NVIDIA board's announcement that it doesn't plan to bring Jensen back squashed the stock's attempted rebound, which began on rumors of the rock-star CEO's possible return.

Interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed NVIDIA's commitment to supporting AI infrastructure financing but promised greater selectivity and discipline in future investments and guarantees. Markets inferred that there would be much less financing and fewer backstops for the weaker AI names and AI startups, as NVIDIA continues confronting its own mess, stretching well beyond leadership uncertainty – and even beyond SEC, FBI, and congressional investigations.

One notable fallout from the Jensen Huang controversy was the sudden urgency within the U.S. government to crack down on semiconductor export loopholes, which allowed Chinese AI developers to access cutting-edge U.S. AI chips remotely through data-center leasing. The U.S. Commerce Department now requires re-export licenses for markets including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. As of now, the extent of that gray-bordering-on-black market demand remains unknown, but it's likely far from negligible. A slate of media reports has tied China's frontier progress directly to two channels: remote access to NVIDIA's most powerful AI accelerators via Malaysian and Singaporean data centers, and hardware and training data smuggled to China through third countries, with the help of actors like the now-infamous Megaspeed.

The fear is that tighter export controls will lower chip demand and depress prices – which over time would lead to lower investment and even an earnings slowdown. Adding to the anxiety, President Trump promised to impose massive taxes on U.S. companies building data centers abroad to prevent crucial tech from falling into Chinese hands. The iShares Semiconductor ETF's (SOXX) slide accelerated, wiping out over 17% during the week and extending its drawdown from its June peak to roughly 43%. Even if Friday turns out to have been a trough, this will still go down as one of the toughest chip selloffs of all time.

Anthropic's (ANT) historic IPO managed to do two opposite things at once: confirm that the AI narrative is alive and well and leave much of the AI trade bleeding. The Nasdaq debut briefly lifted the Claude maker's market cap above $2 trillion, sucking in institutional and retail flows that rotated out of other tech names to fund ANT allocations. But while the AI lab raised an extraordinary amount of money, the party didn't last long. Bearish tech sentiment prevailed, and the stock had shed more than 20% from its opening pop by Friday's close. Below the surface of Anthropic's mind-blowing frontier-model capabilities and surging revenues lie the same hard questions that have been weighing on the trade for the past few months: when will surging demand for AI compensate for the eye-popping costs of data centers, chips, networking equipment, and electricity needed to power the technology?

Companies across the AI industry are spending hundreds of billions to build and run AI infrastructure before they see a return on that investment on their bottom lines. And that's happening at a time when the macro setup has driven financing costs higher, while lenders are becoming increasingly reluctant to bankroll tech capex without checking thoroughly under the hood. The risk isn't confined to a few neoclouds merging or going out of business – it's a more systemic one: less access to financing means fewer orders for the chipmakers and equipment suppliers counting on the AI buildout. A slower and/or more expensive data-center expansion means frontier-model development and training may face even higher costs. Between the anti-data-center backlash and the hawkish Fed minutes, that risk is becoming more material by the hour.

Which brings us back to the question: how much of NVIDIA's role as the "AI central bank" will disappear? And it doesn't center on financing alone, although roughly $165 billion in backstops, commitments, and guarantees – alongside orders, direct investments, and more – were among the key supports of the AI buildout. Beyond money, Jensen Huang's currency in the AI trade was confidence. Just like a central banker, NVIDIA's cofounder could stabilize a momentary wobble in the trade with words alone. While NVIDIA may continue providing its guarantees and financing to a large extent, the "Godfather of AI" is gone for good.

Currently, the stars have aligned quite negatively for the AI trade and for the broader tech stocks, which have more or less coalesced around the narrative in the past few years. Given the unprecedented weighting of technology in broad-market indexes and the growing alignment of previously non-tech industries – like utilities and builders – with technology, a flagging tech trade should weigh heavily on the stock market in general, with few, if any, insulated niches. A bear market is one small jolt away.

Still, there's hope. Stocks are extremely oversold, and the so-called "Fear & Greed Index" is pointing to extreme fear. All this while the U.S. economy is growing at a solid clip, unemployment is near historic lows, and the S&P 500 companies are reporting their strongest EPS growth in any quarter outside post-crisis rebounds, having beaten estimates for 13 consecutive quarters. Meanwhile, the average forward P/E of the tech sector has collapsed to its lowest since March 2020. The AI revolution is now undoubtedly facing one of its biggest tests to date, if not the biggest one. However, the market appears to be pricing in a far more pessimistic outcome than what the underlying fundamentals currently suggest. Unless something unexpectedly breaks, this is a perfect setup for a powerful bounce.
data.author: Yulia Vaiman

data.title: Quantum Computing's Next Breakthrough Could Be in Energy as Quantinuum (QNT) Joins the Push
data.description:
Quantum computing may finally be getting closer to solving real-world problems, and the energy industry could be one of the first to benefit. Companies including Quantinuum (QNT), Phasecraft, and ORCA Computing are testing ways to use quantum technology to improve power grids, develop better solar cells, and make hydrogen production more efficient.

The importance stems from the fact that this work could finally bring the sector into commercial use while some of its most ambitious goals, including drug discovery, remain years away.

For investors following quantum computing stocks, the shift toward energy offers something worth paying attention to: potential customers with real problems to solve and money to save.

On Friday, amid the broad selloff in tech stocks, QNT stock faced a relatively kind session, losing merely 0.79% to close at $27.74. Nevertheless, the stock is down about 46% in the last three months.

Phasecraft Claims Its Software Can Solve Grid Problems 1,000 Times Faster

One company making progress is British quantum software developer Phasecraft, which has partnered with the U.K.'s National Energy System Operator (NESO).

The two are working on ways to manage electricity networks more efficiently, including deciding how power should move across the grid and which sections should be isolated during emergencies.

Phasecraft says its software can solve certain optimization problems up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing methods.

That's an impressive claim, although the benchmark does not include the time needed to run the quantum algorithm itself. The work is still being tested, and a commercial speed advantage has yet to be established.

The potential savings are easy to see. Power companies need to balance electricity supply and demand constantly, a task becoming more complex as renewable energy use grows. More efficient grid management could reduce operating costs and help utilities get more value from existing infrastructure.

Phasecraft, which raised $34 million in funding in 2025, is also expanding into the U.S. The company announced plans in September to establish its American headquarters in Arlington, Virginia.

Quantinuum and ORCA Computing Are Targeting Energy, Too

Phasecraft isn't alone in chasing the opportunity. Quantinuum, which went public on Nasdaq in June 2026, is using quantum technology to study materials for hydrogen fuel cells. The company is also working with partners to develop materials that could improve carbon capture.

Another British company, ORCA Computing, has teamed up with energy giant BP (BP) to study how molecules behave. The research could help improve biofuels and make them burn more efficiently.

ORCA has also worked with Japanese software company JIJ, BP, and the U.K.'s National Quantum Computing Center on a more practical problem: deciding which power generators to turn on or off to meet electricity demand at the lowest cost.

Quantum Computing Could Also Help Make Solar and Hydrogen Cheaper

The potential applications go beyond electricity grids. Phasecraft is working with solar cell maker Oxford PV to explore new materials that could make solar panels more efficient. It has also joined forces with Johnson Matthey (JMPLY), Harvard University, and quantum hardware developer QuEra to research better catalysts for hydrogen production.

The goal is to reduce the need for iridium, a rare and expensive metal used in certain hydrogen production technologies.

The project is being overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), adding another source of support for quantum research in the energy sector.

For quantum computing companies, these partnerships offer a chance to prove their technology can solve problems that already cost energy businesses money.

The financial payoff, though, is still uncertain. The projects have not established how much commercial revenue quantum companies could earn or when their technology might be widely adopted.

Phasecraft's reported speed gains and Quantinuum's materials research offer promising areas to explore. Turning that progress into repeatable, paid services will provide a more meaningful measure of how close quantum computing is to becoming a commercially useful technology.

Is QNT Stock a Good Investment?

According to TipRanks data, Quantinuum has a Strong Buy consensus, based on 11 Buy ratings issued in the past three months. The average QNT stock price target stands at $63.82, implying about 130% upside from the last closing price.

data.title: Nvidia (NVDA) Faces New Supply Chain Fears as Elon Musk Warns of Lost Deals Without Jensen Huang
data.description:
Nvidia Corporation (NVDA) may be facing another big problem following Jensen Huang's sudden departure as CEO. According to Elon Musk's X post, some of the AI-chip giant's most important business relationships relied on personal trust and handshake agreements rather than traditional contracts. Now, investors are left wondering whether those deals can survive without Huang.

Elon Musk, whose companies Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX buy Nvidia chips, has warned that many critical supply chain relationships depended on Huang personally and that some could be lost now that he's gone.

The concern goes beyond Nvidia's leadership crisis. Huang spent more than three decades building relationships with chip suppliers and major customers, helping Nvidia secure the manufacturing capacity needed to dominate the AI market.

If some of those arrangements are difficult to maintain, Nvidia could face higher costs or tougher competition for future chip supplies.

Meanwhile, on Friday, NVDA stock plunged 14% to close at $125.53.

Nvidia's Supply Chain Was Built on Trust

One of the clearest examples is Nvidia's relationship with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM), which manufactures Nvidia's advanced chips. Earlier this year, Huang revealed that the two companies had done decades of business without an overarching formal contract. Instead, their relationship largely relied on mutual trust and a shared understanding of future demand.

That approach helped Nvidia move quickly as demand for AI chips exploded. Huang also persuaded suppliers to invest in extra capacity by sharing his expectations for how large the AI market could become. Those relationships gave Nvidia an advantage in securing the components needed for its chips.

But personal trust becomes harder to rely on when the person behind it suddenly leaves.

Nvidia Says Its $390 Billion in Commitments Is Secure

Nvidia's new leadership is trying to calm those concerns. During the company's latest earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said operations were continuing normally and that customers and suppliers remained supportive.

She also highlighted Nvidia's $390 billion in purchase commitments, showing that the company has substantial formal arrangements in place.

That distinction is significant. Nvidia isn't operating entirely on handshake agreements. Many existing orders and supply commitments are documented, helping protect near-term operations.

The company also maintains close ties with TSMC and other manufacturing partners, which remain central to its AI-chip production plans.

Can Nvidia Keep Its Edge Without Huang?

Despite public calls from Musk and other prominent figures to bring Huang back, Nvidia's board has rejected the idea of reinstating him as CEO. That leaves Kress and the company's next permanent leader with an important task: maintaining relationships that Huang spent decades building.

Nvidia's existing commitments provide some reassurance, but future negotiations could prove more difficult. Suppliers may seek better terms, especially as other technology companies compete for limited manufacturing capacity.

For investors, the financial impact may eventually show up in Nvidia's gross margins rather than an immediate loss of chip shipments. If securing new manufacturing capacity becomes more expensive without Huang's personal influence, Nvidia could face higher costs even as AI demand remains strong.

The $390 billion in existing commitments helps protect today's business. The more revealing question is whether Nvidia can secure its next round of supply agreements on similarly favorable terms.

Is NVDA Stock a Buy?

According to TipRanks data, Nvidia carries a Moderate Buy consensus, based on 44 ratings issued in the past three months. The average NVDA stock price target stands at $232.59, implying about 85% upside from the current price.

data.title: Quantum Computing Stocks Sink as Investors Brace for Key Inflation Data Next Week
data.description:
Quantum computing stocks continued their downward spiral on Friday, as investors pulled back from high-risk technology stocks ahead of key U.S. inflation data due Wednesday, November 25. The report could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision and add to the pressure on the sector. Rigetti Computing (RGTI) plunged 11.17%, D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) dropped 10.81%, Quantum Computing Inc. (QUBT) lost 9.84%, and IonQ (IONQ) fell 8.76%.

The losses came as the Nasdaq (NDX) sank more than 5%, with investors pulling back from AI and other high-growth technology stocks. Concerns about rising interest rates and the massive amounts being spent on AI have made investors less willing to take risks, leaving quantum computing companies particularly exposed.

The damage has been building for months. Over the past three months, Rigetti shares have plunged 56.26%, IonQ has lost 49.54%, and QUBT has fallen 46.60%. D-Wave suffered the heaviest decline, losing 65.10% in the past three months.

Interestingly, all four stocks managed to recover some ground in after-hours trading on Friday. Rigetti gained 3.49%, D-Wave rose 3.37%, IonQ climbed 4.22%, and QUBT added 2.50%. Whether those gains can hold when markets reopen Monday is another question.

Why Quantum Computing Stocks Are Falling So Hard

The selloff comes at an uncomfortable time for quantum computing companies. Many are making progress with their technology, but they are still spending heavily to turn that progress into a profitable business.

IonQ recently reported strong revenue growth, reaching $173.8 million in the third quarter, up 336% from a year earlier. Yet the company also posted an adjusted EBITDA loss of $133.6 million, showing how expensive that growth remains.

D-Wave faces a similar challenge. Its third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $4.5 million, but operating expenses jumped 84% to $55.9 million. Bookings also fell 19% to $1.9 million, raising questions about how quickly customer demand is turning into new business.

Those numbers have become more important as investors rethink the prices they are willing to pay for companies with large future growth expectations but limited profits today.

Higher interest rates add to the pressure, since they can reduce the present value of earnings investors expect years down the road. For smaller quantum companies, continued losses also raise concerns about how much more funding they may need before their businesses become self-sustaining.

What Should Quantum Investors Expect Next Week?

The coming week could bring more volatility, particularly as Wall Street tries to recover from one of its worst weeks in years. On Monday, November 23, the November manufacturing and services PMI reports will offer an early look at U.S. business activity.

Wednesday, November 25, will be particularly important. The U.S. is scheduled to release October's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, along with updated third-quarter GDP figures and weekly jobless claims.

Stronger-than-expected inflation could increase expectations for another Fed rate hike in December, potentially putting more pressure on speculative technology stocks. A softer inflation reading, on the other hand, could help ease some of that pressure.

The trading calendar adds another wrinkle. U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and will close early at 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, November 27. With fewer trading hours and potentially lighter volume, sharp price swings could continue.

After losing between roughly 47% and 56% over three months, IonQ, Rigetti, and QUBT may attract bargain hunters. Yet lower share prices alone won't resolve concerns about cash burn, future funding needs, or the time required to reach profitability.

Wednesday's inflation figures could provide an early indication of whether the pressure on high-risk technology stocks is likely to ease before the Fed's December 8-9 meeting.

We used TipRanks' Comparison Tool to align all four pure-plays appearing in the piece. It's a great tool for investors to get an in-depth view of each stock to better understand the broader quantum sector.

data.title: CrowdStrike (CRWD) in Talks to Buy Zscaler (ZS), Sending Shares in Opposite Directions
data.description:
CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is reportedly in talks to acquire Zscaler (ZS), a deal that could bring together two cybersecurity giants worth a combined $267 billion. Currently, discussions are ongoing, and an agreement could come soon. Nothing is final yet, though, and the companies could still walk away.

Investors were quick to react. Zscaler shares jumped about 16% in after-hours trading on Friday after the report, while CrowdStrike stock fell over 10% in combined trading and after-hours trading. Zscaler had a market value of around $32 billion before the news broke, making this potentially one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever.

Neither company has publicly confirmed the talks or commented on the potential deal.

Why CrowdStrike Wants Zscaler

CrowdStrike is already a major name in cybersecurity, best known for its Falcon platform, which protects computers, laptops, and servers from cyberattacks.

However, Zscaler brings something different to the table. Its cloud-based security platform helps companies control who can access their networks and applications. It also offers an alternative to traditional virtual private networks (VPNs), which have repeatedly been targeted by hackers.

Put the two together, and CrowdStrike could offer companies a much broader security system. It would gain more visibility into activity across devices, applications, and corporate networks, making it easier to spot and block suspicious behavior. That could be a big selling point as businesses face growing threats from AI-powered cyberattacks.

Zscaler already has an impressive customer base. The company serves around 11,000 customers worldwide, including more than half of the Fortune 500, and operates across more than 185 countries.

Its revenue reached a record $3.35 billion in fiscal 2026, although it has yet to post an annual profit since going public in 2018.

Zscaler shares have fallen more than 13% this year, partly amid concerns that AI tools could make traditional software products easier and cheaper to replace. Its large customer base and established security network, however, could be difficult for competitors to replicate.

A $244 Billion Cybersecurity Market Is Getting Bigger Deals

The potential acquisition comes as the cybersecurity industry goes through a wave of consolidation. Companies are spending billions to expand their security platforms as AI makes cyberattacks more complex and businesses look to work with fewer security providers.

Alphabet's Google (GOOGL) struck a $32 billion deal to acquire cloud security company Wiz last year. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) completed its $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in February and recently agreed to buy AI software company Applied Compute for $4.5 billion.

ServiceNow (NOW) also agreed to acquire cybersecurity company Armis for $7.75 billion in December 2025.

The money flowing into the industry is substantial. Research firm Gartner (IT) expects global information security spending to reach $244 billion this year, up nearly 12% from 2025.

There's also a new challenge emerging. As AI agents take on more tasks without human involvement, security companies need better ways to tell legitimate automated activity from malicious traffic.

That makes the combination of CrowdStrike's device protection and Zscaler's network security technology particularly interesting.

What Could a Zscaler Acquisition Mean for CrowdStrike?

At a market value of roughly $235 billion, CrowdStrike is much larger than Zscaler. Still, buying a company worth $32 billion would be a major financial commitment, especially since acquisitions typically come with a premium over the target's share price.

CrowdStrike would also face the challenge of bringing two large security platforms together while maintaining service quality for thousands of corporate customers.

That task carries particular weight given CrowdStrike's history. In July 2024, a faulty software update from the company triggered a global IT outage, disrupting airlines, banks, hospitals, and other businesses.

The possible deal could help CrowdStrike compete more directly with Palo Alto Networks and other companies offering a broad range of cybersecurity services.

But the financial details will be crucial. Zscaler's $3.35 billion in annual revenue gives CrowdStrike an established business to potentially add to its platform, yet Zscaler remains unprofitable on an annual basis.

Without an agreed purchase price or financing plan, investors cannot yet assess the impact on CrowdStrike's earnings, cash flow, or potential share dilution. Those details would help determine whether the proposed acquisition makes financial sense for its shareholders.

We used TipRanks' Comparison Tool to compare both companies and better understand their financial standing.

data.title: Amazon (AMZN) Eyes $7.5 Billion AI Startup Deal as Nvidia Rivalry Heats Up
data.description:
Amazon (AMZN) is reportedly close to buying Israeli AI startup Decart for $7.5 billion, as the tech giant looks for new ways to compete with Nvidia (NVDA). According to the Financial Times, talks are at an advanced stage, and a deal could be announced as soon as early next week. Nothing is signed yet, though, and the negotiations could still fall apart.

Decart makes software that helps AI models run faster while using less computing power. That's a pretty useful skill these days, especially for Amazon Web Services (AWS), which is spending heavily on its own AI chips.

The reported $7.5 billion price tag is also a big jump for Decart. The startup was valued at $4 billion in May after raising $300 million from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark, Radical Ventures, and Nvidia itself.

On Friday, amid the broad selloff in tech stocks, AMZN stock lost 4.10% to close at $246.82.

Why Amazon Wants Decart

Amazon has been working to loosen Nvidia's grip on the AI chip market. In late 2025, AWS launched its Trainium3 chip, designed to compete with Nvidia's widely used graphics processing units (GPUs).

Decart was one of the first companies to use Trainium3 to power its products, so the two already have some history together. The startup's technology tackles a major headache for AI companies: getting enough computing power to run increasingly complex models.

Its software helps AI models do more work with fewer chip resources. That means AWS could potentially serve more customers without having to keep adding expensive hardware.

And with tech companies pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure, squeezing more performance out of existing chips is becoming a big deal.

Decart also has a more creative side. Its products include Lucy, which lets users edit videos in real time, and Oasis, which can generate interactive virtual worlds using AI.

Founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, the company has grown quickly and now operates its U.S. headquarters in San Francisco.

Amazon Keeps Spending as AI Stocks Take a Hit

The timing is interesting. U.S. technology stocks just had their worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, with the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) dropping 10.4% as investors grew nervous about the massive sums being spent on AI.

Amazon, though, doesn't appear ready to slow down. Earlier this year, the company agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar for $11.5 billion. It also paid $8.4 billion for movie studio MGM back in 2022.

A Decart acquisition could give AWS another tool to compete with Nvidia, particularly as demand for AI computing power keeps growing.

The obvious catch is the price. At $7.5 billion, Amazon would be paying nearly twice Decart's valuation from just six months ago. The startup's revenue and profits haven't been disclosed, so it's hard to tell how quickly the investment might pay off.

For now, the companies are still negotiating. If the deal goes through, Amazon would gain software that already runs on its Trainium3 chips, potentially helping AWS get more value from the hardware it has spent years developing.

What Is the Price Target for AMZN Stock?

According to TipRanks data, Amazon has a Strong Buy consensus, based on 43 analysts' ratings issued in the past three months. The average AMZN stock price target stands at $325.02, implying about 32% upside from the current price.

data.title: The Week That Was, The Week Ahead: Macro and Markets, November 22
data.description:
U.S. stocks suffered a brutal selloff this week, with Nvidia Corporation (NVDA) leading the decline as fresh regulatory concerns added to the turmoil surrounding the AI-chip giant. The broader market also came under pressure from rising interest rate fears, even as Anthropic (ANT) made its long-awaited Wall Street debut in one of the largest IPOs in history.

The S&P 500 (SPY) fell 8.6% for the week, its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, while the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) dropped 10%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) lost 8%, as investors pulled back from technology stocks and other risky assets.

Friday brought another round of heavy selling. The S&P 500 plunged 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, entering correction territory after falling more than 10% from its October 6 record high. The Nasdaq sank 5.61% to 25,028.98, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93% to 48,147.33.

The declines wiped out much of the market's gains for the year. The Nasdaq is now down 2.7% in 2026, while the S&P 500 and Dow are barely holding on to positive returns.

Market sentiment also took a hit. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, jumped to 35.89, reflecting a sharp rise in expected market volatility.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield ended the week near 4.91%, down from roughly 5.15% a week earlier as investors moved toward government bonds. Gold (CM:XAUUSD) fell to around $3,539 per ounce, while oil (CM:CL) traded near $83.62 per barrel. Bitcoin (BTC-USD) hovered around $58,868.

The selling was widespread. More than 8,300 stocks declined during the week, compared with about 1,500 gainers. Even some of the market's biggest names struggled to escape the downturn.

Nvidia Faces SEC Probe as Shares Extend Their Selloff

Nvidia Corporation (NVDA) remained at the center of Wall Street's troubles this week, with shares falling 22.9% over five trading sessions. The stock plunged another 14% on Friday as investors reacted to reports of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into the company's accounting practices.

According to Reuters, SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. The investigation adds to the pressure facing the company following the sudden resignation of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The leadership crisis began the previous week, when Huang resigned amid scrutiny over his reported ties to a businesswoman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement.

Reports that Nvidia is moving away from the Chinese market added another concern for investors. China has long been an important market for AI chips, and any lasting loss of sales could put further pressure on the company's growth outlook.

Anthropic's $83 IPO Makes a Huge Splash on Wall Street

AI developer Anthropic (ANT) made its highly anticipated Nasdaq debut on Thursday, November 19, after pricing its initial public offering at $83 per share, above its previously expected range of $70 to $78.

The stock opened at $111.50, jumping more than 34% above the IPO price as investors rushed to buy shares. The early excitement faded during the session, but Anthropic still closed its first trading day at $97.17, a gain of about 17%. However, the stock dropped another 8.50% on Friday, closing at $88.91.

Additionally, Anthropic announced on Friday that it had completed its offering, selling 1.127 billion shares at $83 each. The IPO generated about $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, including shares sold by existing investors.

The company also completed a separate $26 billion private placement involving major technology companies, including Microsoft (MSFT), Google (GOOGL), Nvidia, AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO). Together, the transactions generated approximately $119.5 billion in gross proceeds.

The timing was far from ideal. Anthropic's debut took place during one of the toughest weeks for technology stocks in years, and its shares came under pressure on Friday as the broader market continued to slide.

Fed Signals More Interest Rate Hikes as Inflation Remains Stubborn

The Federal Reserve added to market concerns this week after minutes from its October 27-28 meeting pointed toward further interest rate increases.

The minutes, released Wednesday, showed that nearly all policymakers expected another quarter-point rate increase in December. Some officials even discussed the possibility of a larger hike.

The Fed held its benchmark rate near 3.9% in October after raising rates in September. With inflation still running above the central bank's 2% target, officials appear reluctant to ease their stance.

Core inflation has been running near 3.5%, with price pressures spreading across both goods and services. The minutes also showed concern that inflation could remain elevated longer than previously expected.

Higher rates create another obstacle for stocks, particularly technology companies whose valuations depend heavily on expected future profits.

They also raise borrowing costs for businesses and consumers. Mortgage rates above 7% have already weighed on the housing market, while concerns about household spending continue to grow.

Investors now face the prospect of another rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, even as the stock market struggles to regain its footing.

Disney Targets $3 Billion in Annual Savings After Strong Earnings

The Walt Disney Company (DIS) announced plans to cut roughly $3 billion in annual operating costs by fiscal 2029, even as its latest quarterly results topped Wall Street's expectations.

Disney reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $25.9 billion, up 16% from $22.5 billion a year earlier. Adjusted earnings rose to $1.77 per share from $1.11, helped by stronger theme park attendance and solid demand for sports programming.

The company also plans to increase content spending by 9% in its next fiscal year, bringing the total to approximately $26 billion.

The cost-cutting program is expected to include additional job reductions, following earlier rounds of layoffs. The company has not yet detailed exactly how the $3 billion in annual savings will be distributed across its businesses. That breakdown will help determine how much of the benefit reaches operating profit.

FAA Investigates Nationwide Flight Ground Stop

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) continued investigating the nationwide flight ground stop that disrupted U.S. air travel on Friday, November 13.

The agency halted departures after technical problems affected its communications network, creating concerns about the stability of air traffic control systems.

According to the FAA, the problem involved older equipment becoming unstable as its network was flooded with connection attempts.

The restrictions were lifted after roughly five hours, but the disruption left airlines dealing with delayed flights and a backlog of passengers.

The incident raised concerns about the resilience of aging aviation infrastructure. The FAA's findings could eventually influence technology upgrades and spending priorities across the air traffic control system.

The Week Ahead: Thanksgiving, Fed Expectations, and the AI Selloff

Wall Street heads into a shortened trading week with plenty to digest after the sharp decline in stocks.

U.S. markets will be closed on Thursday, November 26, for Thanksgiving, while trading on Friday, November 27, will end early at 1 p.m. Eastern Time.

The Federal Reserve's next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, leaving investors focused on fresh economic data and comments from central bank officials.

The market will also be watching Nvidia and Anthropic. Nvidia faces unresolved questions about its accounting investigation and leadership transition, while Anthropic enters its first full week as a public company following a record-breaking IPO.

One figure stands out as the new week begins: the S&P 500 ended Friday more than 11% below its October record, with the Nasdaq down roughly 18% from its own peak. That leaves technology stocks particularly exposed to further selling if rate expectations rise or new concerns emerge around the AI sector.

Upcoming Earnings and Ex-Dividend Announcements

data.title: Nvidia or Palantir: Billionaire Andrew Law Sold One AI Stock Before the Crash, Made a $123 Million Bet on the Other
data.description:
Investors are probably spending this weekend recovering from Wall Street's worst week since April 2025. The S&P 500 plunged 8.6%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered a 10% loss. And some of the best-known names in AI have taken a serious beating; Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has now lost about 47% of its value since its October peak, while Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) has fallen 31% from its own high that month.

So, what's driving this meltdown? Investors have been hit by one problem after another. The Democrats' Blue Wave election victory has raised fears of tougher AI regulations and restrictions on data center construction. Meanwhile, the scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, followed by his resignation, has dealt another blow to confidence in the tech sector. Add China's regulatory tensions to the mix, and semiconductor stocks have even more to worry about.

And just when investors were hoping for some relief, Anthropic's blockbuster IPO failed to deliver. Initially viewed as a potential turning point for the struggling tech sector, the highly anticipated debut did little to restore confidence, with Anthropic shares tumbling 8.5% on Friday, just one day after the company went public. Add persistent inflation, and hawkish Federal Reserve commentary pointing toward higher interest rates, and it's easy to understand why investors are nervous.

But history also offers a reason to look beyond the panic. Buying stocks when fear dominates Wall Street has rewarded patient investors time and again, although finding the right opportunities is never easy. That brings us back to Nvidia and Palantir. With both AI giants trading far below their October highs, which one looks like the better buy today?

For billionaire investor Andrew Law, the answer appears to be Palantir. Law, a hedge fund manager and philanthropist who serves as chairman, CEO, and a leading shareholder of Caxton Associates, made some revealing moves involving these two AI stocks ahead of the market's latest collapse. Let's take a closer look at Caxton's third-quarter 13F filing to see just how aggressively Law traded them and what Wall Street analysts see ahead.

Nvidia

Nvidia investors have just endured a week they would probably prefer to forget. The AI chip giant suffered its worst weekly performance since October 2008, during the height of the global financial crisis, with shares plunging 23%. The historic sell-off followed a series of setbacks, including the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, mounting investigations, tighter restrictions on chip exports to China, fears of tougher AI regulations following the Democrats' election victory, and growing concerns about spending on AI.

Luckily for billionaire investor Andrew Law, he managed to avoid much of the damage before Nvidia's collapse. During the third quarter, Law's Caxton Associates slashed its position by 99%, unloading 1,008,726 NVDA shares ahead of the crash.

Yet, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest that the company's underlying growth story remains very much alive. For the fiscal third quarter, revenue surged 103% year-over-year to $115.84 billion, exceeding Wall Street's $109.33 billion forecast. Adjusted earnings also came in ahead of expectations at $2.68 per share, compared with estimates of $2.48. Data center sales reached $107.6 billion, beating projections of $101.87 billion, while the company generated $43.77 billion in free cash flow.

And the outlook was equally encouraging, with Nvidia forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above analysts' $125.3 billion estimate. Interim CEO Colette Kress also raised the fiscal 2028 sales growth projection to 75%, compared with the previous forecast of 70%. Meanwhile, the company ended the quarter with $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization, providing considerable financial flexibility.

But again, the strong results have done little to calm investors worried about Nvidia's leadership crisis. During the earnings call, Chairman Harvey Jones confirmed that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, while refusing to discuss the circumstances surrounding his resignation or the ongoing investigation. That leaves investors facing an uncertain future, despite the company's continued ability to deliver record financial results.

With Nvidia trading far below its October peak, many bulls would argue that the current valuation represents a screaming buy. However, top Evercore analyst Mark Lipacis, who ranks among the top 1% of Wall Street analysts, believes the stock could become even cheaper before its recovery begins.

"Despite a beat and raise quarter, we remain In Line as we believe CEO vacuum, internal/external investigations cap upside to P/E ratio… We've argued that P/E ratios typically compress in the late innings of the cycle when EPS exceed previous peak levels, YY revenues decelerate and supply chain inventories build. We expect the combination of succession overhang and investigation uncertainty to offset any potential multiple relief from fundamental support and continued capital returns. Accordingly, while 11x NTM P/E sits ~46% below the 10-year trough average, we continue to expect a derate to as low as 8x," Lipacis opined.

That In Line (i.e., Neutral) rating, however, comes with a $184 price target, which still implies about 47% upside from current levels. But for Lipacis, even that potential return isn't enough to justify the risks he sees at this stage. (To watch Lipacis' track record, click here)

Turning to the rest of the Street, most analysts remain bullish despite Nvidia's recent troubles. The stock holds a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 30 Buys, 13 Holds, and just one Sell issued over the past three months. The average price target of $232.59 suggests an 85% upside from current levels. (See NVDA stock forecast)

Palantir

The ongoing Wall Street crash has also been unforgiving to Palantir. The AI software leader, known for its powerful data analytics platforms and growing role in enterprise AI, fell another 6.6% on Friday amid widespread selling in tech stocks. Concerns about elevated valuations, growing uncertainty surrounding AI spending, and signs of slower commercial bookings have left investors wondering how much further the stock might fall.

Yet, billionaire investor Andrew Law saw big potential in Palantir before the latest market meltdown. During the third quarter, his hedge fund initiated a new position, purchasing 856,221 PLTR shares worth about $123 million at current prices. The move suggests Law was willing to bet on the company's longer-term prospects, despite the risks surrounding its valuation. And a look at Palantir's latest financial results offers some compelling reasons for that confidence.

For the third quarter, Palantir delivered adjusted earnings of $0.44 per share on revenue of $2.31 billion, representing a 96% year-over-year increase. Both figures exceeded Wall Street's expectations of $0.41 per share and $2.18 billion in sales. Meanwhile, U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government sales of $953 million for the first time in the company's history.

Looking ahead, Palantir expects fourth-quarter revenue between $2.649 billion and $2.653 billion, well above analysts' $2.46 billion forecast. The software developer also raised its full-year sales outlook to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, exceeding the Street's $8.2 billion estimate.

Still, the stock fell following those results as slowing U.S. commercial bookings raised concerns about whether such rapid expansion could continue.

One Wall Street analyst who remains convinced of Palantir's potential is Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges. She maintains a Buy rating on PLTR stock, accompanied by a $235 price target that implies about 64% upside from current levels. Her bullish outlook rests largely on the growing adoption of sovereign AI and evidence that customers are expanding their initial software contracts into much larger commitments. (To watch Borges' track record, click here)

"We think Palantir is very well positioned with Sovereign AI, which will likely be the next phase of enterprise AI transformation in 2027. The key will be converting shorter duration contracts into longer duration commitments, which Palantir has done successfully in the past. Annualized USC ARPC reached ~$5.7mn, up ~20% qoq and 90% yoy. Recent pilots have scaled roughly 5-15x in ACV, including: a global athletic company from $1.6mn to ~$21mn; a home appliance company from $1mn to $15mn as usage broadened across commercial, finance and supply chain; and an apparel company from $2.5mn to $11.5mn. In our view, this demonstrates how tangible ROI can translate into broader deployments and continued wallet share expansion. Taken together, while we do not expect further acceleration, we do believe that growth can be sustained at very high levels over the next several quarters, driving 20-35% upside to 2029 Street revenue estimates," Borges commented.

Looking beyond Goldman Sachs, the outlook for Palantir remains largely positive among Wall Street analysts. Of the 26 recommendations published over the past three months, 19 are Buys, compared with 5 Holds and only 2 Sells, giving PLTR a Moderate Buy consensus rating. Meanwhile, the average price target of $229.09 suggests shares could climb almost 60% over the coming year. (See PLTR stock forecast)
